---
title: "Perceptual representations and efficient encoding"
description: "Representation learning, rate–distortion compression, and the perceptual prior as a mechanism for controlling coding complexity under partial observability."
toc-depth: 3
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- Under limited processing capacity, a perceptual encoder must balance retaining
  distinctions useful for decisions against code complexity; minimizing
  complexity alone admits an uninformative channel.
- A learned normalized perceptual prior controls variational coding cost: for a
  fixed encoder and input distribution, improving the prior reduces prior
  mismatch in the coding bound without changing how much information the
  representations retain.
- Temporal prediction and sensory reconstruction are candidate
  representation-learning objectives, but neither avoiding collapse nor
  achieving a good variational bound guarantees that the retained distinctions
  support good decisions.
:::

In the [POMDP agent architecture](pomdp-rl.qmd#model-components), the
perceptual channel $F(z\mid x) = P(Z = z \mid X = x)$ determines which
distinctions in a sensory input $x$ reach the policy and memory update as a
latent $z$. Mapping two observations that call for different actions (given the
same memory) to the same latent distribution prevents the policy from
distinguishing them; conversely, preserving every sensory detail spends limited
biological capacity on irrelevant variation.

Rate--distortion theory frames this trade-off between retained information and
compression error [@sims2016], treating information rate as a surrogate for code
complexity. Because minimizing complexity alone collapses $F$ to an
uninformative channel, capacity control must be paired with a task-performance
or distortion requirement.

## Efficient encoding and the perceptual prior

### Perceptual prior

To measure and control coding cost, we introduce a learned perceptual prior
$R_\theta(z)$ (also called a latent prior) describing which representations are
likely. In the first-version scope, $R_\theta$ captures structure within a
single latent without taking temporal history as an explicit input, although its
parameters $\theta$ accumulate past experience. It must be a normalized
probability mass function or density rather than an arbitrary scalar score,
defining latent surprise (negative log-likelihood) as

$$
  \ell_\theta(z) = -\log R_\theta(z).
$$

### Measuring information

Given a policy-induced input distribution $p(x)$ and encoder $F(z \mid x)$, the
aggregate latent distribution is

$$
  q_F(z) = \int p(x)F(z \mid x)\,dx.
$$

The mutual information $I_F(X;Z)$ quantifies how much the latent representation
reveals about sensory input. By the variational rate identity underlying
@alemi2018, the expected KL divergence from $F(\cdot \mid X)$ to $R_\theta$
upper-bounds this information rate:

$$
  \mathcal C(F,\theta)
  = \mathbb E_X D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(F(\cdot \mid X)\Vert R_\theta\big)
  = I_F(X;Z) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_F\Vert R_\theta\big)
  \ge I_F(X;Z).
$$

Expected KL therefore decomposes into information rate plus prior mismatch. For
fixed $F$ and $p(x)$, an unrestricted prior minimizes $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ by
matching $q_F$ and closing the gap, whereas a restricted parametric prior may
leave positive mismatch. Crucially, improving $R_\theta$ reduces prior mismatch
without changing $I_F(X;Z)$. Treating $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ as biological
coding cost is a modeling hypothesis: the identity alone does not establish a
biological mechanism that exploits $R_\theta$ to achieve coding savings.

### Capacity constraint and complexity penalty

Suppose the encoder's information rate is limited by capacity $K$, so that
$I_F(X;Z) \le K$. Enforcing the tractable bound $\mathcal C(F,\theta) \le K$
guarantees that this capacity limit holds, but a mismatched prior makes the
constraint unnecessarily tight. Improving $R_\theta$ for a fixed encoder and
input distribution lowers $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ toward $I_F(X;Z)$ without
discarding sensory distinctions, motivating prior learning as a way to control
code complexity. ([Rate--distortion and prior
mismatch](rate-distortion-prior.qmd) illustrates this vertical drop above a
rate--distortion curve on an exact binary channel.)

For $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ and $I_F(X;Z)$ to be finite, $R_\theta$ must cover
the support of $q_F$ and continuous deterministic encoders may require noise or
quantization; base-2 logarithms yield bits and natural logarithms yield nats.

## Representation learning

Capacity control alone cannot specify which sensory distinctions matter. Two
candidate families of objectives push $F$ to retain information without directly
supervising on downstream task reward.

### Learning by temporal prediction

The predictive learning rule of @halvagal2023 operates entirely in latent space,
without reconstructing sensory input: predictive plasticity draws
representations of temporally adjacent inputs together to promote invariance,
while Hebbian plasticity preserves variance across activity to prevent collapse.
Preserving variance, however, does not guarantee that the encoder distinguishes
situations that require different actions.

### Learning by reconstruction

A variational autoencoder pairs the encoder with a decoder $p_\psi(x \mid z)$.
Under $p(x)F(z \mid x)$, following @alemi2018 [Eqs. 2--6], reconstruction
distortion is $\mathcal D = \mathbb E[-\log p_\psi(X \mid Z)]$, and jointly
minimizing $\mathcal D + \beta \mathcal C(F,\theta)$ over encoder, decoder, and
prior trades reconstruction fidelity against variational coding cost for
$\beta \ge 0$ (recovering the expected negative ELBO at $\beta = 1$). The choice
of decoder likelihood determines which errors are penalized---for instance, a
fixed-variance isotropic Gaussian yields squared error up to scale and offset.

When entropy and log-loss are well-defined, $H(X) - \mathcal D \le I_F(X;Z)$, so
beating the best input-independent reconstruction loss requires informative
latents. A good ELBO by itself does not: an expressive decoder can ignore $Z$,
and positive $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ can reflect prior mismatch rather than
retained information. Rate and distortion must therefore be evaluated
separately, alongside whether the policy can use the resulting latents on its
task. Which training stimuli, likelihood, architecture, and compression weight
$\beta$ preserve decision-relevant distinctions remains an empirical question.

## Isolating prior learning

During joint training of $F$ and $R_\theta$, updates to $F$ shift the aggregate
latent target $q_F$, and reducing $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ alone would invite
encoder collapse. To study prior learning in isolation, we can assume $F$ has
already acquired useful representations, freeze its parameters (a stop-gradient
equivalent), and train only $R_\theta$. Under a fixed input distribution $p(x)$,
training $R_\theta$ then minimizes only the prior mismatch
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_F \Vert R_\theta)$ while $I_F(X;Z)$ stays constant.

In a POMDP, however, changing which stimuli the agent attends changes $p(x)$ and
thus shifts $q_F$. Updating $R_\theta$ from trajectories collected under a
sampling policy different from the target policy therefore requires correcting
for that distribution shift. How an agent might optimize a behavioral policy to
sample trajectories for learning $R_\theta$ is developed in the [computational
model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd).
